name: Hydrogen

discovery.note: Cavendish made it by dropping metals into acid and showed it burns to form water; Lavoisier named it in 1783.

nameOrigin: Greek hydro (water) + genes (forming): it makes water when it burns.

radioactive.note: Tritium, used in glowing exit signs and fusion research.

elementalForm.description: Two hydrogen atoms each share their single electron, making one shared pair: a single covalent bond. With that pair both atoms have the helium-like full first shell.

allotropes.name: Orthohydrogen and parahydrogen
allotropes.note: Two forms of H2 that differ only in whether the two nuclear spins are parallel or opposite.

bulk.note: Solid hydrogen is a crystal of H2 molecules.

originNote: Almost all hydrogen formed in the first minutes and hundreds of thousands of years after the Big Bang.
appearance: Colorless, odorless gas; glows pink-violet in an electric discharge.
summary: Hydrogen is the simplest and most common element: one proton and one electron. It makes up about three-quarters of the ordinary matter in the universe and powers the stars by fusing into helium.
uses: Fuel cells and rocket fuel (liquid hydrogen)
facts: About 74% of the ordinary mass in the universe is hydrogen.
A hydrogen atom without its electron is just a proton.
Every water molecule contains two hydrogen atoms.
biology: Essential: part of water, all organic molecules and DNA; about 10% of human body mass.
hazards: Extremely flammable; mixtures with air from 4% to 75% hydrogen can explode.

name: Helium

discovery.note: Seen as an unknown yellow line in the Sun's spectrum during an eclipse; found on Earth by William Ramsay in 1895.

nameOrigin: Greek helios, the Sun, where it was first detected.

elementalForm.description: Helium's two electrons completely fill its only shell, so its atoms have no reason to share or exchange electrons. It forms no stable compounds under ordinary conditions and exists as single atoms.

bulk.structure: Hexagonal close-packed (only under pressure above 25 atm)
bulk.note: At normal pressure helium stays liquid down to absolute zero.

originNote: Most helium was made in the Big Bang; stars add more by fusing hydrogen.
appearance: Colorless gas; glows orange-pink in a discharge tube.
summary: Helium is the second lightest and second most abundant element in the universe. It is so unreactive and so weakly attracted to itself that it never freezes at normal pressure.
uses: Cooling superconducting magnets in MRI scanners
Lifting gas for balloons and airships
facts: Liquid helium below 2.17 K becomes a superfluid that can creep up the walls of its container.
Almost all helium on Earth comes from radioactive alpha decay in rocks and is collected from natural gas.
hazards: Not toxic, but breathing pure helium displaces oxygen and can cause suffocation.

name: Lithium

discovery.note: Found in the mineral petalite; William Brande first isolated the metal by electrolysis of lithium oxide in 1821, and Bunsen and Matthiessen made larger amounts in 1855.

nameOrigin: Greek lithos, stone, because it was found in a mineral.

elementalForm.description: Each lithium atom gives its one outer 2s electron to a shared sea of electrons. The positive Li+ cores are held together by that negative sea: metallic bonding.

originNote: A little lithium came from the Big Bang; more came from cosmic rays splitting heavier nuclei and from some aging stars.
appearance: Soft, silvery-white metal that tarnishes quickly in air.
summary: Lithium is the lightest metal and the least dense solid element: it floats on water (while reacting with it). It is the key ingredient in rechargeable batteries.
uses: Lithium carbonate as a mood-stabilizing medicine
facts: Lithium is so light it would float on oil.
It burns with a crimson-red flame.
biology: No essential role known; lithium salts treat bipolar disorder.
hazards: Reacts with water to release flammable hydrogen; causes burns.

name: Beryllium

discovery.note: Found as an oxide in beryl and emerald; the metal was isolated in 1828 by Wöhler and Bussy.

nameOrigin: From beryl, the mineral it was found in.

radioactive.note: Made by cosmic rays in the air; used to date ice and sediments.

elementalForm.description: Beryllium atoms pool their two 2s electrons in a shared electron sea. Its bonding has more directional, covalent character than most metals, which makes it stiff and brittle.

originNote: Almost all beryllium was made when cosmic rays smashed into carbon, nitrogen and oxygen nuclei in space.
summary: Beryllium is a very light but extremely stiff metal. It is nearly transparent to X-rays, which makes it valuable for windows in X-ray tubes and detectors.
uses: Mirrors of the James Webb Space Telescope (gold-coated beryllium)
Copper-beryllium spring alloys and non-sparking tools
facts: Emerald and aquamarine are both varieties of the beryllium mineral beryl.
Beryllium is about six times stiffer than steel for its weight.
hazards: Inhaled beryllium dust can cause chronic beryllium disease, a serious lung illness.

name: Boron

discovery.by: Joseph Louis Gay-Lussac; Louis Jacques Thénard; Humphry Davy
discovery.note: Isolated impure from boric acid; pure boron was only made in 1909.

nameOrigin: From borax, the mineral it was extracted from (Arabic buraq).

elementalForm.description: Boron has only three valence electrons, too few for ordinary pairs everywhere. Its atoms form B12 icosahedra held together by multi-center bonds, where one electron pair is shared by three atoms.

allotropes.name: Beta-rhombohedral boron
allotropes.note: The most stable form, built from linked B12 icosahedra.

allotropes.name: Alpha-rhombohedral boron
allotropes.note: A simpler packing of single icosahedra.

allotropes.name: Amorphous boron
allotropes.note: A brown powder.

bulk.note: A very complex structure; the viewer shows one B12 icosahedron.

originNote: Like lithium and beryllium, boron was made mostly when cosmic rays split larger nuclei.
appearance: Black-brown lustrous crystals or brown powder; extremely hard.
summary: Boron is a metalloid with too few electrons to bond in ordinary ways, so it builds icosahedral clusters. Boron compounds make heat-proof glass, hard abrasives and detergents.
uses: Boron fibers and boron carbide armor
Control rods in nuclear reactors (boron-10 absorbs neutrons)
facts: Boron carbide is one of the hardest known materials.
Boron-10 captures neutrons so well it is used in cancer therapy.
biology: Essential for plants (cell walls); trace amounts may help human bone health.
hazards: Elemental boron is of low toxicity; some boron compounds such as boranes are highly toxic.

name: Carbon

discovery.note: Charcoal and soot have been used since prehistory; Lavoisier showed diamond is carbon in 1772.

nameOrigin: Latin carbo, charcoal.

radioactive.note: Made by cosmic rays in the air; used for radiocarbon dating.

elementalForm.description: In graphite each carbon shares electron pairs with three neighbors in flat hexagonal sheets, and its fourth electron is delocalized across the sheet, so graphite conducts electricity. In diamond each carbon shares a pair with four neighbors in a rigid 3D network.

allotropes.name: Graphite
allotropes.note: Stacked sheets of hexagons; soft, black and conductive.

allotropes.name: Diamond
allotropes.note: A 3D tetrahedral network; the hardest natural material.

allotropes.name: Graphene
allotropes.note: A single sheet of graphite one atom thick.

allotropes.name: Fullerenes (C60)
allotropes.note: Hollow football-shaped molecules.

allotropes.name: Carbon nanotubes
allotropes.note: Graphene rolled into tubes.

bulk.note: Carbon sublimes at about 3,915 K at normal pressure instead of melting.

originNote: Made by fusing three helium nuclei in stars, then spread by aging stars and supernovae.
appearance: Black, soft graphite or clear, very hard diamond.
summary: Carbon can share electrons with up to four partners, including other carbon atoms, so it forms chains, rings and networks. That makes it the backbone of millions of compounds and of all known life.
uses: Fuels: coal, oil and natural gas are carbon compounds
Diamonds for cutting tools and jewelry
Graphite in pencils, batteries and lubricants
facts: More compounds contain carbon than any other element except hydrogen.
Diamond and graphite are the same element, just bonded differently.
biology: The basis of all organic molecules; about 18% of human body mass.
hazards: Carbon itself is of low toxicity; fine soot and dust harm the lungs.

name: Nitrogen

discovery.note: Found as the part of air that would not support burning or life after carbon dioxide was removed.

nameOrigin: Greek nitron + genes: 'forming niter' (saltpeter).

elementalForm.description: Each nitrogen atom shares three of its five outer electrons, giving three shared pairs: a triple bond. Each atom keeps one lone pair. The triple bond is one of the strongest bonds known, which makes N2 very unreactive.

originNote: Made by the carbon-nitrogen-oxygen fusion cycle in stars.
appearance: Colorless, odorless gas; a clear liquid below 77 K.
summary: Nitrogen makes up 78% of the air. Its triple bond is hard to break, so living things depend on special bacteria, lightning and the Haber process to turn it into usable compounds.
uses: Inert atmosphere for food packaging and electronics
Liquid nitrogen for freezing and cryogenics
facts: About 78% of each breath you take is nitrogen.
Liquid nitrogen boils at −196 °C.
biology: Essential: in every amino acid, protein and DNA base.
hazards: Not toxic, but can displace oxygen and suffocate; liquid nitrogen causes frostbite.

name: Oxygen

discovery.note: Scheele made it around 1771–72 but published only in 1777; Priestley made it in 1774 and published in 1775.

nameOrigin: Greek oxys (sharp, acid) + genes (forming): Lavoisier wrongly thought all acids contain it.

elementalForm.description: Two oxygen atoms share two electron pairs, a double bond, and each keeps two lone pairs. The full picture is subtler: O2 has two unpaired electrons, which makes liquid oxygen magnetic.

allotropes.name: Dioxygen (O2)
allotropes.note: The oxygen we breathe.

allotropes.name: Ozone (O3)
allotropes.note: A bent three-atom molecule that shields Earth from ultraviolet light.

originNote: Made by helium fusion inside massive stars and scattered by their supernovae.
appearance: Colorless gas; pale blue as a liquid and solid.
summary: Oxygen is the most abundant element in Earth's crust and the third most abundant in the universe. It pulls electrons strongly, so it combines with almost every element and drives burning and breathing.
facts: Liquid oxygen is attracted to magnets.
Almost half of the mass of Earth's crust is oxygen, mostly locked in rocks.
biology: Essential: used by cells to release energy; about 65% of human body mass.
hazards: Pure oxygen makes fires burn far more fiercely.

name: Fluorine

discovery.note: Isolated by electrolysis after decades of attempts that injured or killed several chemists; Moissan won the 1906 Nobel Prize.

nameOrigin: From the mineral fluorite (Latin fluere, to flow), used as a flux.

radioactive.note: Used in FDG for PET cancer scans.

elementalForm.description: Two fluorine atoms share one electron pair, a single bond, and each keeps three lone pairs. The bond is weak because the lone pairs crowd each other, which is one reason fluorine is so reactive.

originNote: Made in small amounts in massive stars and some aging stars; fluorine is easily destroyed in stellar cores.
appearance: Pale yellow gas; yellow liquid below 85 K.
summary: Fluorine is the most electronegative element: it pulls electrons harder than any other. It reacts with nearly everything, even glass and some noble gases.
uses: Fluoride in toothpaste and drinking water
facts: Fluorine can react with xenon, a 'noble' gas.
Water, glass and steel wool can burn in a stream of fluorine.
biology: Fluoride strengthens tooth enamel; not known to be essential.
hazards: Extremely toxic and corrosive gas; reacts violently with most substances.

name: Neon

discovery.note: Found by distilling liquefied air; its bright red glow was the first clue.

nameOrigin: Greek neos, new.

elementalForm.description: Neon's second shell is full (8 electrons), so its atoms neither share nor exchange electrons. No stable neutral neon compound is known.

bulk.note: Atoms held only by weak van der Waals forces.

originNote: Made by carbon fusion in massive stars.
appearance: Colorless gas; glows red-orange in a discharge tube.
summary: Neon is a noble gas famous for the red-orange glow of neon signs. It is the least reactive of all elements.
facts: Pure neon glows red-orange; most other sign colors come from other gases, mercury vapor, colored glass or coatings.
Neon is the fifth most abundant element in the universe but rare on Earth.
hazards: Harmless except as a suffocation risk in enclosed spaces.

name: Sodium

discovery.note: Isolated by passing electricity through molten sodium hydroxide.

nameOrigin: From soda; the symbol Na is from Latin natrium.

radioactive.note: A positron emitter used in research.
Used as a medical and industrial tracer.

elementalForm.description: Each sodium atom releases its single 3s electron into a shared electron sea that binds the Na+ cores. With only one electron per atom the bonding is weak, so sodium is soft and melts at 98 °C.

originNote: Made by carbon fusion in massive stars.
appearance: Soft, silvery metal, easily cut with a knife; tarnishes at once in air.
summary: Sodium is a soft, very reactive metal. It gives up its outer electron so readily that it is never found free in nature, but its ion Na+ is everywhere, from sea salt to nerve signals.
uses: Table salt and many sodium compounds
facts: Sodium reacts with water so vigorously that the hydrogen released can catch fire.
Sodium gives fireworks and street lamps their yellow-orange color.
biology: Essential: Na+ carries nerve impulses and controls body fluid balance.
hazards: Reacts violently with water; causes burns.

name: Magnesium

discovery.note: Black recognized magnesia as a new element's oxide; Davy isolated the metal by electrolysis in 1808.

nameOrigin: From Magnesia, a district in Greece known for magnesium minerals.

elementalForm.description: Magnesium atoms each release two 3s electrons into a shared electron sea around Mg2+ cores.

originNote: Made by carbon and neon fusion in massive stars.
summary: Magnesium is a light, strong metal that burns with a dazzling white flame. It sits at the heart of every chlorophyll molecule.
uses: Lightweight alloys for cars, aircraft and laptops
Antacids and laxatives (magnesium hydroxide and sulfate)
facts: Burning magnesium cannot be put out with water: it keeps burning and releases hydrogen.
Each chlorophyll molecule holds one magnesium ion at its center.
biology: Essential: needed by hundreds of enzymes and by ATP; central to chlorophyll.
hazards: Powder or ribbon is flammable; burning magnesium is very hard to extinguish.

name: Aluminium

discovery.note: Ørsted made impure aluminium in 1825; Friedrich Wöhler made purer metal in 1827.

nameOrigin: From alum (Latin alumen), a salt of aluminium.

radioactive.note: Made in massive stars and supernovae; its gamma rays are seen across the Milky Way. Cosmic rays also make small amounts in rocks and meteorites.

elementalForm.description: Each aluminium atom contributes three valence electrons to the shared electron sea that binds the Al3+ cores.

originNote: Made by carbon and neon burning in massive stars.
summary: Aluminium is the most abundant metal in Earth's crust. It is light and resists corrosion because a thin oxide skin seals its surface.
facts: In the 1850s aluminium was more precious than gold; the tip of the Washington Monument is aluminium.
Recycling aluminium saves about 95% of the energy needed to make it from ore.
hazards: Low toxicity; fine powder is flammable.

name: Silicon

discovery.note: Made by heating potassium fluorosilicate with potassium.

nameOrigin: Latin silex, flint.

elementalForm.description: Like carbon in diamond, each silicon atom shares one electron pair with each of four neighbors, building a 3D tetrahedral network.

originNote: Made by oxygen fusion in massive stars and in white-dwarf explosions.
appearance: Hard, brittle, blue-grey crystals with a metallic shine.
summary: Silicon is a semiconductor and the second most abundant element in the crust, mostly as silica and silicates. Purified silicon crystals are the foundation of computer chips and solar cells.
facts: Sand is mostly silicon dioxide.
Chip-grade silicon is purified to better than 99.9999999%.
biology: Used by diatoms and some plants to build skeletons; trace role in humans uncertain.
hazards: Low toxicity; breathing crystalline silica dust causes silicosis.

name: Phosphorus

discovery.note: Brand boiled down large amounts of urine while searching for the philosopher's stone and got a glowing substance.

nameOrigin: Greek phosphoros, light-bearer, because white phosphorus glows in air.

radioactive.note: Used in biology research and medicine.

elementalForm.description: White phosphorus is made of P4 tetrahedra: each atom shares one pair with each of the other three and keeps one lone pair. The 60° bond angles are strained, which makes white phosphorus very reactive.

allotropes.name: White phosphorus (P4)
allotropes.note: Waxy, glows in air and ignites by itself near 30 °C.

allotropes.name: Red phosphorus
allotropes.note: Chains of linked P4 units; used on match boxes.

allotropes.name: Black phosphorus
allotropes.note: Layered like graphite; the most stable form.

originNote: Made by neon and oxygen burning in massive stars.
appearance: White phosphorus is a waxy, pale solid; red phosphorus is a dark red powder.
summary: Phosphorus is essential to life: it forms the backbone of DNA and the energy carrier ATP. Its pure forms range from dangerously reactive white phosphorus to stable red and black phosphorus.
facts: Phosphorus was the first element discovered by a known person.
Your bones and teeth are mostly calcium phosphate.
biology: Essential: DNA, RNA, ATP, cell membranes and bones.
hazards: White phosphorus is very toxic and ignites spontaneously in air.

name: Sulfur

discovery.note: Known since ancient times as brimstone; Lavoisier recognized it as an element in 1777.

nameOrigin: Latin sulfur (or sulphur), the ancient name.

radioactive.note: Made by cosmic rays; a tracer in biology.

elementalForm.description: Sulfur atoms form crown-shaped rings of eight. Each atom shares one pair with each of its two neighbors in the ring and keeps two lone pairs.

allotropes.name: Rhombic sulfur (alpha-S8)
allotropes.note: The stable yellow crystals at room temperature.

allotropes.name: Monoclinic sulfur (beta-S8)
allotropes.note: Needle crystals stable above 96 °C.

allotropes.name: Plastic sulfur
allotropes.note: Rubbery long chains made by pouring hot sulfur into water.

originNote: Made by oxygen fusion in massive stars and in white-dwarf explosions.
summary: Sulfur is a yellow nonmetal found near volcanoes. Its compounds give rotten eggs and skunks their smell, and sulfuric acid is the world's most-produced industrial chemical.
facts: Jupiter's moon Io is coated in sulfur from its volcanoes.
Molten sulfur turns blood red and thick as it is heated.
biology: Essential: in the amino acids cysteine and methionine and in the vitamins thiamine and biotin.
hazards: Elemental sulfur has low toxicity; burning it forms toxic sulfur dioxide.

name: Chlorine

discovery.note: Scheele made it but thought it contained oxygen; Humphry Davy showed it was an element in 1810.

nameOrigin: Greek chloros, pale green-yellow.

elementalForm.description: Two chlorine atoms share one electron pair (a single bond); each keeps three lone pairs, completing an octet of eight electrons.

originNote: Made by oxygen burning in massive stars.
summary: Chlorine is a reactive halogen that grabs one electron to become the chloride ion in table salt. It kills microbes, which made chlorinated drinking water one of the great public-health advances.
facts: Your stomach makes hydrochloric acid to digest food.
Chlorine was used as a weapon in World War I.
biology: Essential as chloride ion: stomach acid and body-fluid balance.
hazards: Toxic, corrosive gas that damages the lungs.

name: Argon

discovery.note: Found because nitrogen taken from air was slightly heavier than nitrogen made from chemicals.

nameOrigin: Greek argos, lazy or inactive.

radioactive.note: Used to date groundwater and ice.

elementalForm.description: Argon's outer shell holds a full octet, so its atoms stay single. Only one neutral argon compound, HArF, has been made, and only below −246 °C.

originNote: Argon-36 and -38 come from stars; the argon-40 in our air comes from radioactive potassium-40 decaying in rocks.
appearance: Colorless gas; glows lilac in a discharge tube.
summary: Argon is the third most common gas in air (about 0.93%). Being inert, it protects hot metals and filaments from oxygen.
facts: Almost all of Earth's argon came from radioactive potassium.
There is more argon in a room than carbon dioxide.
hazards: Can displace oxygen in enclosed spaces.

name: Potassium

discovery.note: The first metal isolated by electrolysis, from molten potash (potassium hydroxide).

nameOrigin: From potash; the symbol K is from Latin kalium (Arabic qali, plant ashes).

radioactive.note: 0.0117% of natural potassium; the largest source of natural radioactivity in your body; used for potassium-argon dating.

elementalForm.description: Each potassium atom gives its lone 4s electron to the shared electron sea. One loosely held electron per atom makes the metal very soft and very reactive.

originNote: Made by oxygen burning in massive stars.
appearance: Soft, silvery metal that tarnishes within seconds in air.
summary: Potassium is a soft alkali metal more reactive than sodium. As the K+ ion it is vital for every living cell, and it is a main nutrient in fertilizers.
uses: Potassium nitrate in gunpowder and food curing
Potassium hydroxide for soft soaps and batteries
facts: Bananas are rich in potassium, so they are very slightly radioactive.
Potassium reacts with water fast enough to ignite the hydrogen with a lilac flame.
biology: Essential: K+ sets the electrical voltage of nerve and muscle cells.
hazards: Reacts violently with water; can form explosive peroxides in storage.

name: Calcium

discovery.note: Isolated by electrolysis of lime and mercury oxide; lime itself was used since antiquity.

nameOrigin: Latin calx, lime.

radioactive.note: 0.187% of natural calcium; decays so slowly it is almost stable.

elementalForm.description: Calcium atoms each contribute two 4s electrons to the shared electron sea around Ca2+ cores.

originNote: Made by oxygen and silicon burning in massive stars and in white-dwarf explosions.
appearance: Silvery, fairly soft metal that turns grey in air.
summary: Calcium is the fifth most abundant element in the crust and the most abundant metal in the human body. Chalk, limestone, marble, bones and shells are all built from calcium compounds.
uses: Calcium carbonate in chalk, antacids and paper
Alloys and getters in vacuum tubes
facts: About 99% of your body's calcium is in your bones and teeth.
The White Cliffs of Dover are chalk made from the calcium carbonate skeletons of tiny algae.
biology: Essential: bones and teeth, muscle contraction, nerve signals and blood clotting.
hazards: Metal reacts with water to release hydrogen; low toxicity.

name: Scandium

discovery.note: Found in euxenite and gadolinite; Mendeleev had predicted it as 'eka-boron'.

nameOrigin: Latin Scandia, Scandinavia.

radioactive.note: Used as a tracer in oil refineries.

elementalForm.description: Scandium atoms pool their three outer electrons (4s2 3d1) in a shared electron sea.

originNote: Made in the final burning stages of massive stars.
appearance: Soft, silvery-white metal with a slight yellow tint in air.
summary: Scandium is a light transition metal, scattered thinly through many minerals. Small additions make aluminium alloys much stronger.
uses: Aluminium-scandium alloys for sports equipment and aircraft
facts: Its existence and properties were predicted by Mendeleev eight years before it was found.

name: Titanium

discovery.note: Found in ilmenite sand in Cornwall; named by Martin Klaproth in 1795. Pure metal was first made in 1910.

nameOrigin: The Titans of Greek mythology.

radioactive.note: Made in supernovae; seen in the Cassiopeia A remnant.

elementalForm.description: Titanium's four outer electrons (4s2 3d2) join a shared electron sea; partly filled d orbitals add strong, slightly directional bonding.

allotropes.name: Alpha titanium
allotropes.note: Hexagonal, stable below 882 °C.

allotropes.name: Beta titanium
allotropes.note: Body-centered cubic, above 882 °C.

originNote: Made in supernovae of both main kinds.
summary: Titanium is as strong as steel but about 45% lighter, and it resists corrosion. Most of it is used as titanium dioxide, the bright white pigment in paint and sunscreen.
uses: Titanium dioxide white pigment and sunscreen
facts: Bone grows onto titanium implants, a process called osseointegration.
biology: None known; the body tolerates it extremely well.
hazards: Low toxicity; fine powder can burn.

name: Vanadium

discovery.note: Del Río found it in Mexico but was persuaded it was chromium; Nils Sefström rediscovered it in 1830.

nameOrigin: Vanadís, a Norse goddess of beauty, for its colorful compounds.

elementalForm.description: Vanadium contributes five valence electrons (4s2 3d3) to strong metallic bonding.

originNote: Made mainly in white-dwarf (type Ia) supernovae.
summary: Vanadium is a hard metal mostly added to steel for toughness. Its ions show four different colors in solution, one for each oxidation state.
uses: Vanadium redox-flow batteries for grid storage
Vanadium pentoxide catalyst for sulfuric acid
facts: Some sea squirts concentrate vanadium in their blood cells a million-fold.
biology: Used by some organisms; possibly beneficial in trace amounts for humans.
hazards: Vanadium compounds, especially the pentoxide, are toxic.

name: Chromium

discovery.note: Found in the red mineral crocoite (lead chromate).

nameOrigin: Greek chroma, color, for its brightly colored compounds.

radioactive.note: Used to label red blood cells.

elementalForm.description: Chromium has six valence electrons (3d5 4s1, an exception to the usual filling order). Its half-filled d shell gives strong metallic bonding and a high melting point.

originNote: Made mostly in white-dwarf supernovae.
summary: Chromium is a hard, shiny metal that resists tarnish. Adding it to iron makes stainless steel, and traces of it make rubies red and emeralds green.
uses: Pigments such as chrome green and chrome yellow
facts: Rubies are red because of a little chromium in aluminium oxide.
biology: Trivalent chromium was long thought essential; this is now doubted.
hazards: Hexavalent chromium compounds are toxic and carcinogenic.

name: Manganese

discovery.note: Isolated by reducing manganese dioxide with carbon.

nameOrigin: From magnesia nigra (black magnesia), via Italian manganese.

radioactive.note: Made in supernovae and by cosmic rays.

elementalForm.description: Manganese contributes seven valence electrons, but its half-filled d shell holds them unusually tightly, giving a complex, brittle crystal.

allotropes.name: Alpha manganese
allotropes.note: Complex cubic cell with 58 atoms, stable at room temperature.

allotropes.name: Beta manganese
allotropes.note: Complex cubic cell with 20 atoms, 727–1095 °C.

allotropes.name: Gamma manganese
allotropes.note: Face-centered cubic, 1095–1133 °C.

allotropes.name: Delta manganese
allotropes.note: Body-centered cubic, 1133 °C up to melting at 1246 °C.

bulk.note: The real cell is very complex; the viewer shows a simplified body-centered cubic packing.

originNote: Made mainly in white-dwarf (type Ia) supernovae.
summary: Manganese is essential to steelmaking and to life. Its compounds include the deep purple oxidizer potassium permanganate.
facts: Photosynthesis splits water using a cluster of four manganese atoms.
biology: Essential: needed by many enzymes, including the water-splitting center of photosynthesis.
hazards: Long-term inhalation of manganese dust or fumes damages the nervous system.

name: Iron

discovery.note: Iron from meteorites was used before 3000 BCE; smelting began in the Bronze Age, by about 2000 BCE, and became widespread around 1200 BCE (the Iron Age).

nameOrigin: Anglo-Saxon iren; the symbol Fe is from Latin ferrum.

radioactive.note: Made in supernovae; found in deep-sea crusts.

elementalForm.description: Iron atoms share 4s and some 3d electrons in a metallic sea. Its unpaired d electrons line up in domains, which makes iron ferromagnetic.

allotropes.name: Alpha iron (ferrite)
allotropes.note: Body-centered cubic, stable below 912 °C; magnetic below 770 °C.

allotropes.name: Gamma iron (austenite)
allotropes.note: Face-centered cubic, 912–1394 °C.

allotropes.name: Delta iron
allotropes.note: Body-centered cubic again above 1394 °C.

originNote: Made as radioactive nickel-56 in supernovae, which decays to iron-56.
appearance: Lustrous grey metal that rusts in moist air.
summary: Iron is the most used metal and, by mass, the most common element on Earth as a whole, since it fills the core. Iron-56 sits near the peak of nuclear stability, so stars cannot gain energy by fusing beyond it.
uses: Steel for buildings, vehicles and tools
facts: The red color of blood and of Mars both come from iron.
When a massive star's core turns to iron, it collapses and explodes as a supernova.
biology: Essential: carries oxygen in hemoglobin and is used by many enzymes.
hazards: Iron overdose is dangerous, especially for children taking iron tablets.

name: Cobalt

discovery.note: Showed that the blue color in glass came from a new metal, not bismuth.

nameOrigin: German Kobold, a goblin: miners blamed goblins for ores that gave off poisonous arsenic fumes.

radioactive.note: Gamma source for radiotherapy and sterilizing food and equipment.

elementalForm.description: Cobalt atoms share 4s and 3d electrons in a metallic sea; unpaired d electrons make it ferromagnetic.

allotropes.name: Hexagonal cobalt
allotropes.note: Hexagonal close-packed, stable at room temperature.

allotropes.name: Cubic cobalt
allotropes.note: Face-centered cubic, stable above about 420–450 °C.

originNote: Made in supernovae.
summary: Cobalt is a hard, magnetic metal used in batteries, superalloys and blue pigments. It sits at the center of vitamin B12.
facts: Cobalt blue glass and ceramics have been made for thousands of years.
biology: Essential as part of vitamin B12.
hazards: Cobalt dust and some compounds are toxic and possibly carcinogenic.

name: Nickel

discovery.note: Isolated from a mineral miners called kupfernickel, 'Old Nick's copper'.

nameOrigin: German Nickel, a mischievous sprite, from the ore that looked like copper but gave none.

radioactive.note: Made in supernovae; decays to iron-56.

elementalForm.description: Nickel atoms share electrons in a metallic sea; partly filled 3d orbitals make it ferromagnetic.

originNote: Made in supernovae.
summary: Nickel is a tough, corrosion-resistant metal used in stainless steel, coins and batteries. Iron meteorites are mostly iron-nickel alloy.
facts: Earth's core is thought to be about 5% nickel.
biology: Used by some plant and microbial enzymes; not shown essential for humans.
hazards: A common cause of skin allergy; some compounds are carcinogenic.

name: Copper

discovery.note: Used for at least 10,000 years; smelted from ores by about 5000 BCE.

nameOrigin: Latin cyprium, 'metal of Cyprus'; symbol Cu from cuprum.

elementalForm.description: Copper (3d10 4s1, an exception) shares its 4s electron in a free-flowing electron sea, which makes it an excellent conductor of electricity and heat.

originNote: Made by neutron capture in massive stars.
appearance: Reddish-orange, shiny metal that turns green over time.
summary: Copper was one of the first metals people used. It conducts electricity better than any metal except silver, so it wires our world.
facts: The Statue of Liberty is green because its copper skin has formed a patina.
Copper is one of only a few metals that are not grey or silvery; others include gold and caesium.
biology: Essential: used by enzymes; octopus and horseshoe-crab blood uses copper instead of iron.
hazards: Excess copper is toxic; copper salts can poison fish.

name: Zinc

discovery.note: Marggraf isolated it in Europe; zinc was smelted in India from about the 12th century.

nameOrigin: German Zink, perhaps from Zinke (prong), for its spiky crystals.

elementalForm.description: Zinc shares its two 4s electrons in a metallic sea; its full 3d shell does not take part, so bonding is weaker and zinc melts at only 420 °C.

originNote: Made in massive stars and their supernovae.
summary: Zinc protects steel from rust by galvanizing and is a key part of brass. It is essential for life, used by hundreds of enzymes.
facts: Zinc ions help hold together 'zinc finger' proteins that read DNA.
biology: Essential: in hundreds of enzymes and DNA-binding proteins.
hazards: Breathing zinc oxide fumes causes 'metal fume fever'.

name: Gallium

discovery.note: Seen as new violet lines in a zinc ore spectrum; Mendeleev had predicted it as 'eka-aluminium'.

nameOrigin: Latin Gallia, France.

elementalForm.description: Solid gallium is unusual: pairs of atoms share a covalent bond (Ga2 units) inside a metallic framework. This weak packing is why it melts in your hand.

bulk.note: The viewer shows a simplified close-packed lattice.

originNote: Made by neutron capture in massive and aging stars.
appearance: Soft, silvery metal that melts at 29.8 °C.
summary: Gallium melts just above room temperature but boils only above 2,400 °C, giving it one of the longest liquid ranges of any element. Gallium compounds power LEDs and fast electronics.
uses: Gallium nitride blue and white LEDs
Gallium arsenide chips and solar cells
facts: Gallium expands when it freezes, like water.
Mendeleev predicted its density before it was measured, and then corrected its discoverer.
hazards: Low toxicity; it attacks and weakens aluminium.

name: Germanium

discovery.note: Found in the mineral argyrodite; Mendeleev had predicted it as 'eka-silicon'.

nameOrigin: Latin Germania, Germany.

radioactive.note: 7.75% of natural germanium; decays by rare double beta decay.

elementalForm.description: Each germanium atom shares one electron pair with each of four neighbors, forming a diamond-like covalent network. The bonds are weaker than silicon's, making germanium a semiconductor with a smaller band gap.

originNote: Made by neutron capture in stars.
summary: Germanium is a semiconductor that made the first transistors in 1947. Today it is used in fiber optics, infrared lenses and radiation detectors.
facts: The first transistor (Bell Labs, 1947) was made of germanium.
hazards: Low toxicity; some compounds are harmful.

name: Arsenic

discovery.note: Arsenic compounds were known in antiquity; Albertus Magnus is credited with isolating the element.

nameOrigin: Greek arsenikon, yellow orpiment (from Persian zarnikh, gold-colored).

elementalForm.description: In grey arsenic each atom shares one pair with each of three neighbors, making puckered layers, and keeps one lone pair. Weak links between layers give it a metallic shine.

allotropes.name: Grey arsenic
allotropes.note: Layered, metallic-looking; the stable form.

allotropes.name: Yellow arsenic
allotropes.note: Made of As4 tetrahedra like white phosphorus; unstable.

bulk.note: Sublimes at 887 K; melts only under pressure (1,090 K at 36 atm). Drawn as a simplified distorted cubic net.

originNote: Made by neutron capture in massive stars.
appearance: Brittle, steel-grey metalloid with a metallic shine.
summary: Arsenic is a metalloid notorious as a poison, yet it is also used in semiconductors and, as arsenic trioxide, to treat a form of leukemia.
uses: Hardening lead in batteries and ammunition
facts: Arsenic sublimes: solid turns straight to vapor at 615 °C.
biology: Toxic to humans; some microbes use arsenic compounds.

name: Selenium

discovery.by: Jöns Jacob Berzelius; Johan Gottlieb Gahn
discovery.note: Found in residue from a sulfuric acid plant.

nameOrigin: Greek selene, the Moon (it resembles tellurium, named after Earth).

elementalForm.description: Grey selenium is made of endless spiral chains: each atom shares one pair with each of its two neighbors along the chain and keeps two lone pairs.

allotropes.name: Grey (trigonal) selenium
allotropes.note: Helical chains; the stable form, a photoconductor.

allotropes.name: Red selenium
allotropes.note: Se8 rings like sulfur.

allotropes.name: Black amorphous selenium
allotropes.note: Glassy.

originNote: Made by neutron capture in massive stars.
appearance: Grey metallic crystals, red powder or black glass, depending on form.
summary: Selenium conducts electricity far better in light than in the dark, which made it useful in early photocopiers and light meters. It is essential in tiny amounts but toxic in larger ones.
facts: Brazil nuts are among the richest food sources of selenium.
biology: Essential: part of the amino acid selenocysteine in antioxidant enzymes.
hazards: Toxic in excess; hydrogen selenide gas is very poisonous.

name: Bromine

discovery.note: Balard found it in salt-marsh brine; Carl Löwig isolated it independently in 1825.

nameOrigin: Greek bromos, stench.

elementalForm.description: Two bromine atoms share one electron pair, and each keeps three lone pairs. Br2 molecules attract each other strongly enough to make bromine a liquid at room temperature.

originNote: Made by neutron capture in massive stars.
appearance: Dark red-brown liquid giving off orange vapor.
summary: Bromine is one of only two elements that are liquid at room temperature; the other is mercury. It is collected from salty brines and the Dead Sea.
facts: Tyrian purple, the ancient dye of emperors, is a bromine compound made by sea snails.
biology: Possibly needed for collagen in animals; studies are ongoing.
hazards: Toxic, corrosive liquid; its vapor burns eyes and lungs.

name: Krypton

discovery.note: Found in the residue left after liquid air boiled away.

nameOrigin: Greek kryptos, hidden.

radioactive.note: 0.355% of natural krypton; decays by rare double electron capture.
Used to date old groundwater and ice.

elementalForm.description: Krypton has a full octet and normally stays as single atoms. With fluorine, the most electron-hungry element, it forms krypton difluoride, KrF2.

originNote: Made by neutron capture in stars.
appearance: Colorless gas; glows white-violet in a discharge.
summary: Krypton is a rare noble gas. From 1960 to 1983 the meter was defined by the wavelength of light from krypton-86.
uses: High-performance light bulbs and flash lamps
facts: Superman's Kryptonite is fictional; real krypton is a harmless gas.

name: Rubidium

discovery.note: Discovered with the new spectroscope from two deep red lines in mineral water and lepidolite.

nameOrigin: Latin rubidus, deep red, for its spectral lines.

radioactive.note: 27.83% of natural rubidium; used in rubidium-strontium dating of rocks.

elementalForm.description: Each rubidium atom gives its single 5s electron to a very weak metallic electron sea; the metal melts at 39 °C.

originNote: Made by neutron capture in stars.
appearance: Very soft, silvery-white metal that ignites in air.
summary: Rubidium is a very reactive alkali metal. Its atoms are the workhorses of atomic clocks and the first Bose-Einstein condensate.
uses: Rubidium atomic clocks (in GPS and phone networks)
facts: The first Bose-Einstein condensate, in 1995, was made from rubidium-87 atoms.
biology: None known; the body treats it much like potassium.
hazards: Ignites in air and reacts explosively with water.

name: Strontium

discovery.note: Recognized in the mineral strontianite; isolated by Humphry Davy in 1808.

nameOrigin: Strontian, a village in Scotland where its ore was found.

radioactive.note: A dangerous fission product that collects in bones.

elementalForm.description: Strontium atoms share two 5s electrons each in a metallic electron sea.

originNote: Mostly made by slow neutron capture in aging stars.
appearance: Soft, silvery metal that yellows in air.
summary: Strontium is a reactive alkaline-earth metal best known for the brilliant red of fireworks. Strontium optical lattice clocks are among the most precise instruments ever built.
facts: Strontium clocks would lose less than a second in the age of the universe.
biology: Not essential; it can replace calcium in bones.
hazards: Stable strontium is of low toxicity; radioactive Sr-90 is dangerous.

name: Yttrium

discovery.note: Found in a black mineral from the Ytterby quarry in Sweden.

nameOrigin: Ytterby, Sweden (which also gave names to ytterbium, terbium and erbium).

elementalForm.description: Yttrium contributes three valence electrons (5s2 4d1) to metallic bonding, like the lanthanides it resembles.

originNote: Made mostly by slow neutron capture in aging stars.
appearance: Silvery metal, fairly stable in air.
summary: Yttrium behaves much like the rare-earth elements. It is the Y in YBCO, a famous high-temperature superconductor, and in YAG lasers.
facts: Moon rocks brought back by Apollo were unusually rich in yttrium.

name: Zirconium

discovery.note: Found as an oxide in zircon; impure metal was isolated by Berzelius in 1824.

nameOrigin: From zircon, Persian zargun, gold-colored.

elementalForm.description: Zirconium contributes four valence electrons (5s2 4d2) to strong metallic bonding.

originNote: Made mostly by slow neutron capture in aging stars.
summary: Zirconium barely absorbs neutrons and resists corrosion, so it clads the fuel rods in nuclear reactors. Zircon crystals are the oldest known pieces of Earth.
facts: Zircon crystals from Western Australia are about 4.4 billion years old.
hazards: Low toxicity; fine powder can ignite.

name: Niobium

discovery.note: Named columbium; confused with tantalum until Heinrich Rose separated them in 1844.

nameOrigin: Niobe, daughter of Tantalus in Greek myth, because it is so like tantalum.

elementalForm.description: Niobium (4d4 5s1) contributes five valence electrons to strong metallic bonding.

originNote: Made by neutron capture in several kinds of stars.
appearance: Grey metal that turns blue, green or violet when anodized.
summary: Niobium becomes superconducting at 9.2 K, the highest of any pure element at normal pressure. Niobium-titanium wire builds the magnets of MRI scanners and the Large Hadron Collider.
facts: About 90% of the world's niobium comes from Brazil.

name: Molybdenum

discovery.note: Scheele showed molybdenite was not graphite; Peter Jacob Hjelm isolated the metal in 1781.

nameOrigin: Greek molybdos, lead, because its ore was confused with lead ore.

radioactive.note: Parent of technetium-99m for medical scans.

elementalForm.description: Molybdenum (4d5 5s1) shares six valence electrons; half-filled d orbitals give very strong metallic bonding and a melting point above 2,600 °C.

originNote: Made by several neutron-capture processes.
summary: Molybdenum is a hard, high-melting metal that strengthens steel. Nitrogen-fixing bacteria depend on a molybdenum enzyme to turn air into fertilizer.
uses: Catalysts for removing sulfur from fuels
facts: Nitrogenase, the enzyme that fixes nitrogen from air, contains molybdenum.
biology: Essential: part of several enzymes in plants, animals and bacteria.

name: Technetium

discovery.note: Found in molybdenum foil bombarded in a cyclotron: the first element made artificially.

nameOrigin: Greek technetos, artificial.

radioactive.note: Used in tens of millions of medical scans each year.

elementalForm.description: Technetium shares its seven valence electrons in metallic bonding, like its neighbors manganese and rhenium.

originNote: All its isotopes are radioactive; tiny traces form naturally in uranium ores, and red giant stars show technetium lines, proving stars make new elements.
summary: Technetium is the lightest element with no stable isotopes. Its metastable isotope technetium-99m is the most widely used medical imaging tracer.
facts: Mendeleev left a gap for it in 1871, but it was only made 66 years later.
biology: None; used only as a diagnostic tracer.

name: Ruthenium

discovery.note: Isolated from platinum ore residues in Kazan.

nameOrigin: Latin Ruthenia, Russia.

elementalForm.description: Ruthenium shares its 4d and 5s electrons in a hard, strong metallic lattice.

originNote: Mostly made by rapid neutron capture in neutron-star mergers.
summary: Ruthenium is a rare, hard platinum-group metal. It makes electrical contacts wear-resistant and is used in important catalysts.
facts: Gottfried Osann reported it in 1827, but Claus was the first to prove it was a new element.
Thin films of ruthenium in an unusual tetragonal form were shown in 2018 to be magnetic at room temperature.
hazards: Ruthenium tetroxide is highly toxic and explosive.

name: Rhodium

discovery.note: Found in platinum ore dissolved in aqua regia.

nameOrigin: Greek rhodon, rose, for its rose-colored salts.

elementalForm.description: Rhodium (4d8 5s1) forms a dense, highly reflective metallic lattice.

originNote: Mostly made by rapid neutron capture.
summary: Rhodium is one of the rarest and most expensive metals. Most of it goes into car catalytic converters, where it breaks down nitrogen oxides.
facts: Rhodium has at times been the most expensive precious metal, over ten times the price of gold.
hazards: Low toxicity as metal; some compounds are harmful.

name: Palladium

discovery.note: Found in platinum ore and first sold anonymously as 'new silver'.

nameOrigin: The asteroid Pallas, discovered a year earlier.

elementalForm.description: Palladium (4d10, with no 5s electron in the free atom) forms a metallic lattice that can soak up hundreds of times its own volume of hydrogen.

originNote: Made by rapid and slow neutron capture.
summary: Palladium absorbs hydrogen like a sponge and is a superb catalyst. Its electron configuration, 4d10 with an empty 5s, is unique.
facts: Palladium can absorb up to about 900 times its own volume of hydrogen.

name: Silver

discovery.note: Mined since at least 3000 BCE in Anatolia.

nameOrigin: Anglo-Saxon seolfor; symbol Ag from Latin argentum.

elementalForm.description: Silver (4d10 5s1) shares its single 5s electron in a very mobile electron sea, which gives it the highest electrical conductivity of any element.

originNote: Made by rapid and slow neutron capture.
summary: Silver conducts electricity better than any other element and heat better than any other metal, and it reflects visible light best of all metals. Silver ions kill bacteria.
facts: Silver tarnish is silver sulfide, formed by sulfur compounds in the air.
biology: None; silver ions are toxic to microbes.
hazards: Low toxicity; long exposure can turn skin blue-grey (argyria).

name: Cadmium

discovery.note: Found as an impurity that colored zinc carbonate yellow.

nameOrigin: Latin cadmia, calamine (zinc ore).

radioactive.note: 12.22% of natural cadmium; a strong neutron absorber.

elementalForm.description: Cadmium shares its two 5s electrons; the full 4d shell stays out, so bonding is weak and cadmium melts at 321 °C.

originNote: Made by slow and rapid neutron capture.
summary: Cadmium is a soft metal used in batteries, pigments and solar cells. It is highly toxic, so many of its uses are being phased out.
facts: Itai-itai disease in 1950s Japan was caused by cadmium-polluted rice.
biology: None in humans; one marine diatom uses a cadmium enzyme.
hazards: Toxic and carcinogenic; damages kidneys and bones.

name: Indium

discovery.note: Found from a brilliant indigo line in the spectrum of zinc ore.

nameOrigin: The indigo line in its spectrum.

elementalForm.description: Indium shares three valence electrons (5s2 5p1) in a soft metallic lattice.

bulk.structure: Body-centered tetragonal (a slightly stretched face-centered cell)
bulk.note: Drawn as a simplified face-centered cubic lattice.

originNote: Made by slow and rapid neutron capture.
appearance: Very soft, silvery metal that cries when bent.
summary: Indium is soft enough to scratch with a fingernail. Indium tin oxide forms the transparent, conductive layer in touchscreens and flat displays.
uses: Indium tin oxide for touchscreens and displays
facts: Bending an indium bar makes a high-pitched 'cry' as its crystals suddenly twin.
hazards: Inhaled indium compounds can harm the lungs.

name: Tin

discovery.note: Used since about 3500 BCE, mainly to make bronze.

nameOrigin: Anglo-Saxon tin; symbol Sn from Latin stannum.

elementalForm.description: White tin is metallic. Below 13 °C it can slowly change into grey tin, a brittle diamond-structure semiconductor where each atom shares pairs with four neighbors.

allotropes.name: White (beta) tin
allotropes.note: Metallic, tetragonal; stable above 13.2 °C.

allotropes.name: Grey (alpha) tin
allotropes.note: Diamond structure, brittle; 'tin pest'.

bulk.note: Drawn as a simplified close-packed lattice.

originNote: Made by slow and rapid neutron capture.
summary: Tin has ten stable isotopes, more than any other element. Mixed with copper it made bronze, and today it is mostly used in solder.
facts: Tin has 10 stable isotopes, the most of any element.
hazards: Metal is low-toxicity; organotin compounds are very toxic.

name: Antimony

discovery.note: Stibnite (antimony sulfide) was used as eye makeup in ancient Egypt.

nameOrigin: Possibly Greek anti-monos, 'not alone'; symbol Sb from Latin stibium.

elementalForm.description: Like grey arsenic, each antimony atom shares pairs with three neighbors in puckered layers and keeps a lone pair; it conducts like a poor metal.

bulk.note: Drawn as a simplified distorted cubic net.

originNote: Made by rapid and slow neutron capture.
summary: Antimony is a brittle metalloid that, like water, expands slightly as it freezes, which made it valuable for casting sharp printing type.
facts: Ancient Egyptians used antimony sulfide as kohl eyeliner.
hazards: Toxic, similar to arsenic but milder.

name: Tellurium

discovery.note: Found in gold ore from Transylvania; named by Klaproth in 1798.

nameOrigin: Latin tellus, Earth.

radioactive.note: 31.74% of natural tellurium: the slowest decay ever measured.

elementalForm.description: Tellurium is built from spiral chains, like grey selenium: each atom shares one pair with each chain neighbor and keeps two lone pairs.

originNote: Made mostly by rapid neutron capture, with some slow capture in aging stars.
summary: Tellurium is one of the rarest stable elements in the crust. Tellurium-128 decays so slowly that its half-life is more than 100 trillion times the age of the universe.
facts: People exposed to tellurium can get strong garlic-smelling breath.

name: Iodine

discovery.note: Seen as violet vapor while making saltpeter from seaweed ash.

nameOrigin: Greek iodes, violet.

radioactive.note: Treats thyroid disease; a hazard in nuclear accidents.
Used in seed implants and lab assays.

elementalForm.description: Two iodine atoms share one electron pair and each keeps three lone pairs. Large, easily distorted I2 molecules attract each other enough to form a solid.

originNote: Made by rapid neutron capture.
appearance: Shiny blue-black crystals that give off violet vapor.
summary: Iodine is a dark solid halogen that turns straight into violet vapor when warmed. Your thyroid needs it to make the hormones that control metabolism.
facts: Iodine deficiency is the world's most preventable cause of brain damage; iodized salt fixed it in many countries.
biology: Essential: part of the thyroid hormones thyroxine (T4) and T3.
hazards: Vapor irritates eyes and lungs; large doses are toxic.

name: Xenon

discovery.note: Found in the last residues of evaporating liquid air.

nameOrigin: Greek xenos, stranger.

elementalForm.description: Xenon has a full octet, but its outer electrons are far from the nucleus. Strongly electron-hungry atoms like fluorine and oxygen can pull them into bonds, forming compounds such as XeF2 and XeF4.

originNote: Made mostly by rapid neutron capture.
appearance: Colorless, very dense gas; glows blue-violet in a discharge.
summary: Xenon was the first noble gas found to form compounds, in 1962. Its bright arc light is used in film projectors and car headlights.
facts: Neil Bartlett's 1962 xenon compound overturned the idea that noble gases cannot react.
biology: None, though it acts as an anesthetic.

name: Caesium

discovery.note: The first element found by spectroscopy, from two blue lines in mineral water.

nameOrigin: Latin caesius, sky blue.

radioactive.note: A major fallout product of Chernobyl and Fukushima.

elementalForm.description: Caesium's single 6s electron is very far from the nucleus and easily shared; the metallic bonding is so weak that caesium melts at 28.5 °C.

originNote: Made by rapid and slow neutron capture.
appearance: Soft, pale-gold metal that melts on a warm day.
summary: Caesium is the most reactive stable metal. The second is defined by the vibrations of caesium-133 atoms: exactly 9,192,631,770 cycles.
uses: Atomic clocks that define the second
facts: Caesium, gold and copper are the only metals that are clearly colored rather than grey or silvery.
hazards: Explodes on contact with water; Cs-137 is a radiation hazard.

name: Barium

discovery.note: Isolated by electrolysis; Carl Scheele had recognized barium oxide in 1772.

nameOrigin: Greek barys, heavy, for the dense mineral barite.

elementalForm.description: Barium shares two 6s electrons per atom in a soft metallic lattice.

originNote: Made mostly by slow neutron capture in aging stars.
appearance: Soft, silvery metal that quickly oxidizes.
summary: Barium is a heavy alkaline-earth metal. Barium sulfate is so insoluble that patients can swallow it safely for X-ray imaging, even though soluble barium salts are poisonous.
uses: Barium sulfate for X-ray imaging and drilling mud
facts: Barium sulfate blocks X-rays, outlining the gut on medical images.

name: Lanthanum

discovery.note: Found hidden in cerium nitrate.

nameOrigin: Greek lanthanein, to lie hidden.

elementalForm.description: Lanthanum contributes three valence electrons (5d1 6s2) to metallic bonding, the pattern shared by most lanthanides.

bulk.note: Real stacking is ABAC (double hcp); drawn as simple hcp.

originNote: Made by slow and rapid neutron capture.
appearance: Soft, silvery-white metal that tarnishes in air.
summary: Lanthanum gives the lanthanide series its name. A hybrid car battery can contain several kilograms of lanthanum.
facts: Lanthanum-nickel alloy can soak up hydrogen like a sponge.
biology: None in humans, but some bacteria, such as ones from volcanic mud pots, use it in an enzyme that breaks down methanol.

name: Cerium

discovery.by: Jöns Jacob Berzelius; Wilhelm Hisinger; Martin Klaproth
discovery.note: Found as an oxide in the mineral cerite.

nameOrigin: The dwarf planet Ceres, discovered in 1801.

elementalForm.description: Cerium's single 4f electron can join the metallic bonding, which lets cerium switch between valences and gives it unusual phase changes.

allotropes.name: Gamma cerium
allotropes.note: Face-centered cubic, stable at room temperature.

allotropes.name: Alpha cerium
allotropes.note: A denser fcc form under pressure or cold.

originNote: Made by slow and rapid neutron capture.
summary: Cerium is the most abundant rare-earth element, more common in the crust than copper. Scraped cerium-iron alloy throws sparks, which is how lighter flints work.
facts: Despite being a 'rare earth', cerium is about as abundant as copper.
biology: None in humans, but some bacteria, such as ones from volcanic mud pots, use it in an enzyme that breaks down methanol.
hazards: Metal can ignite when scratched; low toxicity.

name: Praseodymium

discovery.note: Split 'didymium' into praseodymium and neodymium.

nameOrigin: Greek prasios didymos, green twin, for its green salts.

elementalForm.description: Praseodymium shares three valence electrons; its 4f electrons stay mostly local and give magnetic properties.

originNote: Made by rapid and slow neutron capture.
appearance: Soft, silvery metal that develops a green oxide coat.
summary: Praseodymium is a rare-earth metal used in strong magnets and in yellow-green glass and ceramic colors.
facts: Praseodymium-doped crystals have slowed light to about 45 meters per second in research experiments.
biology: None in humans, but some bacteria, such as ones from volcanic mud pots, use it in an enzyme that breaks down methanol.

name: Neodymium

discovery.note: The 'new twin' separated from didymium.

nameOrigin: Greek neos didymos, new twin.

elementalForm.description: Neodymium shares three valence electrons; its three remaining unpaired 4f electrons stay on each atom and give strong magnetism in compounds.

originNote: Made by rapid and slow neutron capture.
summary: Neodymium makes the strongest permanent magnets known, Nd2Fe14B, found in headphones, wind turbines and electric cars.
facts: A neodymium magnet can lift over 1,000 times its own weight.
biology: None in humans, but some bacteria, such as ones from volcanic mud pots, use it in an enzyme that breaks down methanol.
hazards: Low toxicity; magnets can pinch skin badly.

name: Promethium

discovery.by: Jacob Marinsky; Lawrence Glendenin; Charles Coryell
discovery.note: Identified among uranium fission products at Oak Ridge.

nameOrigin: Prometheus, who stole fire from the gods.

radioactive.note: Used in luminous paint and nuclear batteries.

elementalForm.description: Promethium metal shares three valence electrons like its lanthanide neighbors.

originNote: No stable isotopes; only about half a kilogram exists in Earth's crust at any time, from uranium fission. It is made in reactors.
appearance: Silvery metal; its salts glow pale blue or green from their own radioactivity.
summary: Promethium is the only lanthanide with no stable isotopes. It was finally found among the fission products of the Manhattan Project.
uses: Nuclear batteries for pacemakers and space probes (historically)
facts: In 2024 chemists at Oak Ridge characterized a promethium complex in solution for the first time, almost 80 years after its discovery.

name: Samarium

discovery.note: Found in the mineral samarskite.

nameOrigin: The mineral samarskite, named after Russian mining officer Vasili Samarsky-Bykhovets: the first element named (indirectly) after a person.

radioactive.note: 14.99% of natural samarium; used in samarium-neodymium dating.
13.82%; observationally stable, a strong neutron absorber.

elementalForm.description: Samarium shares three valence electrons in a metallic lattice with an unusual nine-layer stacking.

originNote: Made by rapid and slow neutron capture.
appearance: Silvery metal, fairly stable in air.
summary: Samarium-cobalt magnets keep their strength at high temperatures, making them ideal for aerospace and military motors.
facts: Samarium was the first element named after a person, via the mineral samarskite.

name: Europium

discovery.note: Separated from samarium-gadolinium mixtures.

nameOrigin: Europe.

radioactive.note: 47.81% of natural europium; its extremely slow alpha decay was first reported in 2007 and confirmed in 2014.

elementalForm.description: Europium keeps a half-filled 4f7 shell and shares only two 6s electrons, so it behaves like barium: soft, low-density and very reactive.

originNote: Made almost entirely by rapid neutron capture.
appearance: Silvery metal that oxidizes rapidly in air.
summary: Europium is the most reactive lanthanide. Its glowing compounds made the red of color TV screens and are hidden in euro banknotes as an anti-forgery mark.
uses: Red and blue phosphors in screens and LED lamps
facts: Euro banknotes glow under UV light thanks to europium compounds.

name: Gadolinium

discovery.note: Detected spectroscopically; Lecoq de Boisbaudran purified its oxide in 1886, but the metal was not isolated until 1935.

nameOrigin: The mineral gadolinite, named after Finnish chemist Johan Gadolin.

elementalForm.description: Gadolinium (4f7 5d1 6s2) shares three valence electrons; its seven unpaired 4f electrons make it ferromagnetic just below room temperature.

originNote: Made mostly by rapid neutron capture.
summary: Gadolinium has seven unpaired electrons, which makes its compounds excellent MRI contrast agents. It is ferromagnetic only below 20 °C.
facts: Gadolinium-157 absorbs neutrons better than any other stable isotope.
biology: None; free gadolinium ions are toxic, so MRI agents lock them in cages.
hazards: Free ions are toxic; metal is low hazard.

name: Terbium

discovery.note: Separated from yttria.

nameOrigin: Ytterby, Sweden.

elementalForm.description: Terbium shares three valence electrons; its 4f electrons give strong magnetism.

originNote: Made mostly by rapid neutron capture.
summary: Terbium compounds glow bright green and its alloy Terfenol-D changes shape in a magnetic field more than almost any other material.
uses: Green phosphors in lamps and screens
facts: Terfenol-D stretches noticeably when magnetized, turning magnetic signals into sound.

name: Dysprosium

discovery.note: Took over 30 attempts to separate from holmium oxide.

nameOrigin: Greek dysprositos, hard to get.

elementalForm.description: Dysprosium shares three valence electrons; its many unpaired 4f electrons give one of the largest magnetic moments of any element.

originNote: Made mostly by rapid neutron capture.
summary: A few percent of dysprosium keeps neodymium magnets working at the high temperatures in electric-car motors and wind turbines.
facts: Its name means 'hard to get' because separating it was so difficult.

name: Holmium

discovery.by: Marc Delafontaine; Jacques-Louis Soret; Per Teodor Cleve
discovery.note: Seen spectroscopically and separated from erbia.

nameOrigin: Latin Holmia, Stockholm.

elementalForm.description: Holmium shares three valence electrons; it has the highest magnetic moment of any natural element.

originNote: Made mostly by rapid neutron capture.
summary: Holmium has the strongest magnetic moment of any element and is used to concentrate fields in the most powerful magnets.
uses: Pole pieces for very strong magnets
facts: Holmium oxide glass is a standard for checking spectrometers.

name: Erbium

discovery.note: Separated from yttria along with terbium.

nameOrigin: Ytterby, Sweden.

elementalForm.description: Erbium shares three valence electrons in a hexagonal metallic lattice.

originNote: Made mostly by rapid neutron capture.
appearance: Silvery metal; its salts are pink.
summary: Erbium ions amplify light at 1,550 nm, the wavelength that carries internet signals through optical fibers across oceans.
uses: Erbium-doped fiber amplifiers for the internet
facts: Erbium amplifiers boost light directly, so one undersea fiber can carry many signal colors without converting them to electricity.

name: Thulium

discovery.note: Found in erbia.

nameOrigin: Thule, an ancient name for the far north.

elementalForm.description: Thulium shares three valence electrons in a hexagonal metallic lattice.

originNote: Made by rapid neutron capture.
summary: Thulium is the second rarest lanthanide. Thulium-170 makes compact X-ray sources and its lasers are used in surgery.
facts: Thulium is rare, yet it is more common in the crust than silver.

name: Ytterbium

discovery.note: Separated from erbia.

nameOrigin: Ytterby, Sweden.

elementalForm.description: Ytterbium keeps a full 4f14 shell and shares only two 6s electrons, so its metal is soft and less dense than its neighbors.

originNote: Made by rapid and slow neutron capture.
summary: Ytterbium atoms power some of the most accurate optical atomic clocks. Ytterbium-doped fiber lasers cut and weld metal in industry.
uses: Fiber lasers for cutting and welding
facts: Ytterbium lattice clocks keep time to better than one part in 10^18.

name: Lutetium

discovery.by: Georges Urbain; Carl Auer von Welsbach; Charles James
discovery.note: Three chemists separated it from ytterbia independently.

nameOrigin: Lutetia, the Latin name of Paris.

radioactive.note: 2.599% of natural lutetium; used to date meteorites.
Used in targeted prostate and neuroendocrine cancer therapy.

elementalForm.description: Lutetium (4f14 5d1 6s2) shares three valence electrons; the lanthanide contraction makes it the densest and hardest lanthanide.

originNote: Made by rapid and slow neutron capture.
summary: Lutetium is the last lanthanide. Lutetium-177 is used in modern targeted radiotherapy for prostate cancer.
facts: A 2021 IUPAC project report recommends placing lutetium, not lanthanum, below yttrium in group 3.

name: Hafnium

discovery.note: Found by X-ray spectroscopy in zirconium ore in Copenhagen, guided by Bohr's atomic theory.

nameOrigin: Latin Hafnia, Copenhagen.

radioactive.note: Used to date the formation of planetary cores.

elementalForm.description: Hafnium shares four valence electrons (5d2 6s2). The lanthanide contraction makes it almost the same size as zirconium, so the two are very hard to separate.

originNote: Made by slow and rapid neutron capture.
summary: Hafnium is a near-twin of zirconium but absorbs neutrons strongly. Hafnium oxide insulating layers made modern smaller transistors possible.
facts: Hafnium (1923) was the second-to-last stable element to be discovered; only rhenium (1925) came later.

name: Tantalum

discovery.note: Found in minerals from Finland and Sweden; long confused with niobium.

nameOrigin: Tantalus of Greek myth, tormented in water he could never drink: tantalum oxide does not absorb acid.

radioactive.note: 0.012%: the rarest primordial nuclide and the only primordial nuclear isomer.

elementalForm.description: Tantalum shares five valence electrons in a strong body-centered cubic metallic lattice.

originNote: Made by slow and rapid neutron capture.
summary: Tantalum is extremely corrosion-resistant and forms a tough oxide layer, ideal for tiny high-capacity capacitors in phones and laptops.
facts: Tantalum-180m is the only nuclide found in nature in a long-lived excited state.
biology: None known; very well tolerated by the body.

name: Tungsten

discovery.note: The brothers reduced tungstic acid with charcoal.

nameOrigin: Swedish tung sten, heavy stone; symbol W from wolfram.

elementalForm.description: Tungsten's six valence electrons fill its bonding d states almost exactly, giving the strongest metallic bonding of any element and the highest melting point of any metal.

originNote: Made by slow and rapid neutron capture.
appearance: Steel-grey to white, very dense metal.
summary: Tungsten has the highest melting point of all metals, 3,422 °C. That is why it was used for light-bulb filaments.
uses: Tungsten carbide cutting tools and drill bits
facts: Tungsten is about as dense as gold.
biology: Used by a few heat-loving bacteria; not essential for humans.

name: Rhenium

discovery.by: Walter Noddack; Ida Tacke; Otto Berg
discovery.note: Found by X-ray spectroscopy in platinum ores and gadolinite.

nameOrigin: Latin Rhenus, the Rhine.

radioactive.note: 62.60% of natural rhenium; used in rhenium-osmium dating.

elementalForm.description: Rhenium shares seven valence electrons in a dense hexagonal metallic lattice.

originNote: Made mostly by rapid neutron capture.
summary: Rhenium was the last stable element to be discovered. It has the third highest melting point of any element and is vital to jet-engine turbine blades.
facts: Most natural rhenium is slightly radioactive rhenium-187.

name: Osmium

discovery.note: Found in the black residue left when platinum ore was dissolved in aqua regia.

nameOrigin: Greek osme, smell, for the pungent osmium tetroxide.

elementalForm.description: Osmium's eight valence electrons and the lanthanide contraction pack its atoms extremely tightly.

originNote: Made mostly by rapid neutron capture.
summary: Osmium is the densest naturally occurring element, at 22.59 g/cm³. A cube 10 cm on a side would weigh about 22.6 kg.
uses: Hard alloys for fountain-pen tips and electrical contacts
Osmium tetroxide stain for electron microscopy
facts: Osmium and iridium are so close in density that which is densest depends on how it is measured; osmium usually wins.
hazards: Osmium tetroxide is highly toxic and can blind.

name: Iridium

discovery.note: Found together with osmium in platinum residues.

nameOrigin: Greek iris, rainbow, for the many colors of its salts.

radioactive.note: Gamma source for radiography and brachytherapy.

elementalForm.description: Iridium shares 5d and 6s electrons in a very dense, very hard face-centered cubic lattice.

originNote: Made by rapid neutron capture.
summary: Iridium is the most corrosion-resistant metal. A thin layer rich in iridium, found worldwide in 66-million-year-old rocks, points to the asteroid impact that ended the age of dinosaurs.
facts: The old international prototype kilogram was made of 90% platinum and 10% iridium.

name: Platinum

discovery.by: Antonio de Ulloa (described); used earlier in pre-Columbian South America
discovery.note: Ulloa described it from Colombia; pre-Columbian peoples had already worked it.

nameOrigin: Spanish platina, little silver.

elementalForm.description: Platinum (5d9 6s1) forms a dense, unreactive face-centered cubic metal whose surface is an outstanding catalyst.

originNote: Made by rapid neutron capture.
summary: Platinum is a rare, dense, unreactive metal and one of the most important catalysts, from car exhausts to fuel cells. Platinum compounds such as cisplatin treat cancer.
facts: Platinum does not tarnish even when heated red-hot in air.
Catalytic converters spread platinum as nanoparticles so as much of its surface as possible touches the exhaust.
biology: None; some platinum compounds are anticancer drugs.
hazards: Metal is low-toxicity; some platinum salts cause allergies.

name: Gold

discovery.note: Worked since at least 4000 BCE.

nameOrigin: Anglo-Saxon gold; symbol Au from Latin aurum.

elementalForm.description: Gold (5d10 6s1) shares its 6s electron in a metallic sea. Relativistic effects pull the 6s electron inward, which shifts how gold absorbs light and gives it its yellow color.

originNote: Made by rapid neutron capture, much of it in neutron-star collisions like the one seen in 2017.
summary: Gold resists corrosion and is beautifully yellow because of relativistic effects on its electrons. Much of it was forged when neutron stars collided.
facts: One gram of gold can be beaten into a sheet of about 1 m².
All the gold ever mined would fit in a cube about 22 m on a side.
biology: None; some gold compounds were once used to treat arthritis.

name: Mercury

discovery.note: Found in Egyptian tombs from about 1500 BCE.

nameOrigin: The planet and Roman god Mercury; symbol Hg from hydrargyrum, the Latin form of Greek hydrargyros, water-silver.

elementalForm.description: Mercury's 6s electrons are held so tightly (a relativistic effect) that they barely join the electron sea. The bonding is so weak that mercury is liquid at room temperature.

bulk.note: Drawn as a simplified close-packed lattice.

originNote: Made by slow and rapid neutron capture.
summary: Mercury is the only metal that is liquid at room temperature. Its toxicity has led to bans on most mercury thermometers and many other uses.
facts: Mercury becomes a superconductor below 4.2 K: the first superconductor ever found, in 1911.
biology: None; highly toxic, especially as methylmercury in fish.
hazards: Toxic vapor; methylmercury damages the nervous system.

name: Thallium

discovery.note: Found by a bright green spectral line in sulfuric acid residues.

nameOrigin: Greek thallos, green shoot, for its spectral line.

elementalForm.description: Thallium tends to keep its 6s pair to itself (the 'inert pair effect'), so it often behaves as a +1 metal.

originNote: Made mostly by slow neutron capture.
summary: Thallium is a soft, very toxic metal once used as rat poison. Its compounds are tasteless and odorless, which made it a notorious poison.
facts: Agatha Christie's novel The Pale Horse describes thallium poisoning accurately.

name: Lead

discovery.note: Smelted since at least 6500 BCE.

nameOrigin: Anglo-Saxon lead; symbol Pb from Latin plumbum (as in plumbing).

radioactive.note: From the uranium decay chain; dates recent sediments.

elementalForm.description: Lead's 6s pair is held tightly (inert pair effect), so relatively few electrons bond the metal, making it soft and low-melting.

originNote: Made mostly by slow neutron capture; some comes from the decay of uranium and thorium.
summary: Lead is soft, dense and easy to cast. Lead-208 has a 'doubly magic' nucleus, and it is the end point of the thorium decay chain.
facts: Lead-208 is the heaviest stable nucleus known.
biology: None; toxic, especially to children's brains.

name: Bismuth

discovery.note: Shown to be distinct from lead and tin; it had been used since the 1400s.

nameOrigin: German Wismuth, possibly 'white mass'.

radioactive.note: 100% of natural bismuth; its decay was only detected in 2003.

elementalForm.description: Like arsenic and antimony, each bismuth atom bonds to three neighbors in puckered layers, but the layers are close enough to share electrons, making it a semimetal.

bulk.note: Drawn as a simplified distorted cubic net.

originNote: Made by slow and rapid neutron capture.
appearance: Brittle, pinkish-silver metal; grows rainbow-colored stair-step crystals.
summary: Bismuth is technically radioactive, but its half-life is about a billion times the age of the universe. It is the most diamagnetic metal, repelled by magnets.
facts: Bismuth's rainbow colors come from a thin oxide film, not the metal itself.
biology: None; low toxicity for a heavy metal.

name: Polonium

discovery.note: Found in pitchblende because it was far more radioactive than its uranium.

nameOrigin: Polonia, Latin for Poland, Marie Curie's homeland.

radioactive.note: The natural isotope; used in antistatic devices and notoriously as a poison.

elementalForm.description: Polonium is the only element with a simple cubic crystal: each atom has six neighbors at the corners of cubes.

allotropes.name: Alpha polonium
allotropes.note: Simple cubic.

allotropes.name: Beta polonium
allotropes.note: Rhombohedral, above about 36 °C.

bulk.note: The only element known to crystallize in the simple cubic structure.

originNote: Polonium on Earth is continuously made by the radioactive decay of uranium, whose atoms were forged in merging neutron stars.
appearance: Silvery metal that glows blue from the radiation it emits.
summary: Polonium is intensely radioactive: a gram of polonium-210 heats itself to about 500 °C. It was the first element Marie and Pierre Curie discovered.
uses: Heat source in early space probes
facts: Polonium is the only element with a simple cubic crystal structure.
biology: None; extremely toxic because of its radiation.
hazards: Extremely radiotoxic if swallowed or inhaled.

name: Astatine

discovery.by: Dale Corson; Kenneth MacKenzie; Emilio Segrè
discovery.note: Made by bombarding bismuth with alpha particles at Berkeley.

nameOrigin: Greek astatos, unstable.

radioactive.note: Studied for targeted alpha cancer therapy.

elementalForm.description: No visible amount has ever been made, so its bulk bonding is unmeasured. Calculations suggest it would be a metal rather than forming At2 molecules like the lighter halogens.

originNote: Made briefly in uranium and thorium decay chains; less than a gram exists in Earth's crust at any time.
appearance: Never seen as a bulk sample; it would vaporize from its own radioactive heat.
summary: Astatine is the rarest naturally occurring element, with well under a gram in Earth's crust at any moment. Its properties are mostly inferred from tiny traces and calculations.
uses: Astatine-211 for targeted alpha therapy research
facts: Astatine was made artificially in 1940 and only found in nature afterwards, in 1943.
biology: None; collects in the thyroid like iodine.

name: Radon

discovery.by: Ernest Rutherford; Robert Owens; Friedrich Ernst Dorn
discovery.note: Found as a radioactive gas given off by thorium and radium compounds.

nameOrigin: From radium, which gives it off.

radioactive.note: From the uranium decay chain; the main natural radon.

elementalForm.description: Radon has a full octet and exists as single atoms. Its outer electrons are loosely held, so it can react with fluorine.

originNote: Continuously made by the decay of radium in rocks and soil.
appearance: Colorless gas; solid radon glows from its radioactivity.
summary: Radon is a heavy radioactive gas that seeps from rocks into buildings. After smoking, it is a leading cause of lung cancer in many countries.
facts: Radon is about 8 times denser than air and collects in basements.
hazards: Radioactive; long-term exposure causes lung cancer.

name: Francium

discovery.note: Found at the Curie Institute as a decay product of actinium-227: the last element discovered in nature.

nameOrigin: France, Perey's homeland.

radioactive.note: The longest-lived isotope, from the actinium decay chain.

elementalForm.description: Francium would be an alkali metal sharing one 7s electron in a metallic sea, but no visible amount has ever been made, so this is predicted.

originNote: Exists fleetingly in uranium ores as part of the actinium decay chain; perhaps 20–30 g are in Earth's crust at any time.
appearance: Never seen; the largest sample, about 300,000 atoms, was held in a laser trap.
summary: Francium is the most unstable naturally occurring element. A visible sample would instantly vaporize itself with the heat of its own radioactivity.
uses: Research on atomic structure and the weak nuclear force
facts: It was the last element discovered in nature rather than made in a lab.

name: Radium

discovery.note: Found in pitchblende; Marie Curie and André-Louis Debierne isolated the metal in 1910.

nameOrigin: Latin radius, ray.

radioactive.note: The common natural isotope, from the uranium chain.
Radium-223 dichloride treats prostate cancer spread to bone.

elementalForm.description: Radium shares two 7s electrons per atom in a body-centered cubic metallic lattice, like barium.

originNote: Continuously made in rocks by the decay of uranium and thorium.
appearance: Silvery-white metal that blackens in air; its compounds glow faintly.
summary: Radium glows from its own radioactivity and was once painted on watch dials. Many of the 'radium girls' who painted them suffered severe radiation injuries.
facts: The curie, a unit of radioactivity, was based on one gram of radium-226.
biology: None; it collects in bones like calcium.

name: Actinium

discovery.note: Found in uranium ore residues; Friedrich Giesel found it independently in 1902.

nameOrigin: Greek aktinos, ray.

radioactive.note: The natural isotope, from the uranium-235 chain.
Used in targeted alpha therapy for cancer.

elementalForm.description: Actinium shares three valence electrons (6d1 7s2), like lanthanum above it.

originNote: Made in uranium ores by the decay of uranium-235.
appearance: Silvery metal that glows pale blue in the dark from its radiation.
