summary: Actinium gives the actinide series its name. It is so radioactive that it glows blue in the dark.
facts: A ton of uranium ore contains only about 0.2 mg of actinium.

name: Thorium

discovery.note: Found in a black mineral from Norway (now called thorite).

nameOrigin: Thor, the Norse god of thunder.

radioactive.note: Almost 100% of natural thorium; it decays more slowly than the age of the universe.
Trace; used to date corals and cave deposits.
Its low-energy nuclear transition may enable nuclear clocks.

elementalForm.description: Thorium shares four valence electrons (6d2 7s2) in a face-centered cubic metallic lattice.

originNote: Made by rapid neutron capture; it has survived since before the Sun formed.
appearance: Silvery metal that tarnishes grey to black.
summary: Thorium is about three times more abundant than uranium and is only weakly radioactive. It is studied as a nuclear fuel for thorium reactors.
facts: Much of Earth's internal heat comes from the decay of thorium, uranium and potassium.
hazards: Weakly radioactive; dust is hazardous to inhale.

name: Protactinium

discovery.note: Found as short-lived Pa-234m; Lise Meitner and Otto Hahn found the long-lived Pa-231 in 1918.

nameOrigin: Greek protos (first) + actinium: it decays into actinium.

elementalForm.description: Protactinium shares five valence electrons, partly from 5f orbitals, in a body-centered tetragonal metal.

bulk.note: Drawn as a simplified body-centered cubic lattice.

originNote: Made in uranium ores by the decay of uranium-235.
summary: Protactinium is one of the rarest and most expensive naturally occurring elements, extracted only in tiny amounts.
uses: Research only; Pa-231 is used to date ocean sediments
facts: The largest amount ever purified was about 125 g, extracted from 60 tonnes of waste in the UK in 1961.

name: Uranium

discovery.note: Found as an oxide in pitchblende; Eugène-Melchior Péligot isolated the metal in 1841.

nameOrigin: The planet Uranus, discovered in 1781.

radioactive.note: 99.27% of natural uranium; about the age of Earth.
0.72% of natural uranium; fissile, the fuel of reactors.

elementalForm.description: Uranium's 5f electrons partly join the bonding, giving it an unusual low-symmetry orthorhombic metal structure.

allotropes.name: Alpha uranium
allotropes.note: Orthorhombic, below 668 °C.

allotropes.name: Beta uranium
allotropes.note: Tetragonal.

allotropes.name: Gamma uranium
allotropes.note: Body-centered cubic, above 776 °C.

bulk.note: Drawn as the high-temperature body-centered cubic form.

originNote: Made by rapid neutron capture before the Solar System formed.
appearance: Silvery-grey, very dense metal that tarnishes black.
summary: Uranium is the heaviest element found in large amounts in nature. Splitting uranium-235 nuclei releases enormous energy in nuclear reactors.
uses: Depleted uranium for armor and counterweights
facts: About 2 billion years ago, natural nuclear reactors ran in uranium deposits at Oklo, Gabon.
hazards: Chemically toxic and weakly radioactive; enriched uranium is fissile.

name: Neptunium

discovery.note: Made at Berkeley by bombarding uranium with neutrons: the first transuranium element.

nameOrigin: The planet Neptune, next after Uranus.

radioactive.note: The longest-lived isotope; a nuclear-waste product.

elementalForm.description: Neptunium's 5f electrons take part in bonding, giving a low-symmetry orthorhombic metal.

bulk.note: Drawn as a simplified body-centered cubic lattice.

originNote: Made in reactors; tiny traces form naturally in uranium ores.
appearance: Silvery metal that tarnishes in air.
summary: Neptunium was the first element made beyond uranium. Neptunium-237 is used to make plutonium-238 for spacecraft power sources.
facts: Neptunium has one of the largest liquid ranges of any element: it melts at 639 °C and boils near 4,170 °C.

name: Plutonium

discovery.by: Glenn Seaborg; Edwin McMillan; Joseph Kennedy; Arthur Wahl
discovery.note: Made at Berkeley by bombarding uranium with deuterons.

nameOrigin: The dwarf planet Pluto.

radioactive.note: Fissile; used in reactors and weapons.
Powers spacecraft such as Voyager and Perseverance.

elementalForm.description: Plutonium's 5f electrons sit on the edge between bonding and staying put, which gives it six solid phases, more than any other element.

allotropes.name: Alpha plutonium
allotropes.note: Monoclinic, brittle; stable at room temperature.

allotropes.name: Delta plutonium
allotropes.note: Face-centered cubic; stabilized with gallium for metalworking.

bulk.note: Drawn as the face-centered cubic delta phase.

originNote: Made in reactors; traces form naturally in uranium ores.
appearance: Silvery metal that tarnishes yellow-olive; warm to the touch.
summary: Plutonium is a strange metal with six different solid phases. Plutonium-238 has powered spacecraft for decades, and plutonium-239 is a nuclear fuel.
facts: A piece of plutonium-239 feels warm because of its own radioactive decay.

name: Americium

discovery.by: Glenn Seaborg; Ralph James; Leon Morgan; Albert Ghiorso
discovery.note: Made in a reactor at Chicago by bombarding plutonium with neutrons.

nameOrigin: The Americas, by analogy with europium.

elementalForm.description: In americium the 5f electrons stay on each atom, so it bonds with three valence electrons like a lanthanide.

originNote: Made in nuclear reactors.
summary: Americium-241 is in most household smoke detectors, where its alpha particles ionize the air in a tiny chamber.
facts: A typical smoke detector contains about 0.3 micrograms of americium-241.
hazards: Radioactive; dangerous if swallowed or inhaled.

name: Curium

discovery.by: Glenn Seaborg; Ralph James; Albert Ghiorso
discovery.note: Made by bombarding plutonium-239 with alpha particles.

nameOrigin: Marie and Pierre Curie.

radioactive.note: Alpha source in Mars rover X-ray spectrometers.

elementalForm.description: Curium has a half-filled 5f7 shell and bonds with three valence electrons, like gadolinium.

originNote: Made in nuclear reactors.
appearance: Silvery metal; its compounds glow from their radioactivity.
summary: Curium is intensely radioactive and glows in the dark. Curium-244 sources helped Mars rovers analyze rocks.
uses: Alpha sources for spectrometers on Mars rovers
facts: Its discovery was first announced on a children's radio quiz show in 1945.

name: Berkelium

discovery.by: Stanley Thompson; Albert Ghiorso; Glenn Seaborg
discovery.note: Made at Berkeley by bombarding americium-241 with alpha particles.

nameOrigin: Berkeley, California.

radioactive.note: Used to make heavier elements, including tennessine.

elementalForm.description: Berkelium bonds with three valence electrons in a double hexagonal close-packed metal.

originNote: Made in high-flux reactors.
appearance: Silvery metal; it is made only in milligram batches.
summary: Berkelium is made only in milligram amounts in special reactors. Berkelium-249 was the target used to create tennessine.
facts: The 22 mg of berkelium used to make tennessine took months to produce at Oak Ridge.

name: Californium

discovery.by: Stanley Thompson; Kenneth Street Jr.; Albert Ghiorso; Glenn Seaborg
discovery.note: Made by bombarding curium-242 with alpha particles.

nameOrigin: California and the University of California.

radioactive.note: A strong neutron source: a microgram emits about 2.3 million neutrons per second.

elementalForm.description: Californium bonds with three valence electrons; it is the heaviest element made in amounts large enough to weigh easily.

originNote: Made in high-flux reactors.
summary: Californium-252 is a powerful neutron source used to start nuclear reactors and to find gold, silver and oil underground.
uses: Neutron moisture gauges and oil-well logging
facts: Californium-252 has been priced at tens of millions of US dollars per gram, making it one of the most expensive substances.

name: Einsteinium

discovery.note: Found in debris of the first hydrogen-bomb test, 'Ivy Mike'; kept secret until 1955.

nameOrigin: Albert Einstein.

radioactive.note: The isotope most often made and studied.

elementalForm.description: Einsteinium appears to be divalent in the metal, sharing only two electrons, like europium and ytterbium.

originNote: Made in high-flux reactors and first found in nuclear test debris.
appearance: Silvery metal that glows from its own radiation.
summary: Einsteinium is the heaviest element ever seen as a visible amount. It destroys its own crystal structure with radiation, losing about 3% of its mass each day.
uses: Research only, such as making mendelevium
facts: Its radioactivity is so intense that it glows and damages its own crystal lattice.

name: Fermium

discovery.note: Found with einsteinium in the 'Ivy Mike' hydrogen-bomb debris.

nameOrigin: Enrico Fermi.

elementalForm.description: Only tiny amounts have been made, so the metal has never been studied in bulk. It is predicted to be a divalent metal.

originNote: Made in reactors and by nuclear explosions.
summary: Fermium is the heaviest element that can be made by bombarding lighter elements with neutrons; beyond it, particle accelerators are needed.
facts: Fermium is the last element that can be built up by neutron capture in a reactor.

name: Mendelevium

discovery.by: Albert Ghiorso; Bernard Harvey; Gregory Choppin; Stanley Thompson; Glenn Seaborg
discovery.note: Made by bombarding einsteinium-253 with alpha particles; the first element made one atom at a time.

nameOrigin: Dmitri Mendeleev, creator of the periodic table.

elementalForm.description: Never made in bulk; predicted to be a divalent metal.

originNote: Made in particle accelerators.
summary: Mendelevium was the first element produced and identified one atom at a time; its discoverers found just 17 atoms.
facts: Its discovery experiment produced only 17 atoms.

name: Nobelium

discovery.note: Claimed first in Sweden in 1957; the Dubna work of 1963–66 was credited.

nameOrigin: Alfred Nobel.

elementalForm.description: Never made in bulk; nobelium is unusual in being most stable in the +2 state in water.

originNote: Made in particle accelerators.
summary: Nobelium is a synthetic actinide made atom by atom in accelerators. Unlike most actinides it prefers the +2 oxidation state.
facts: Its discovery was disputed between labs in Sweden, the US and the USSR.

name: Lawrencium

discovery.by: Albert Ghiorso; Torbjørn Sikkeland; Almon Larsh; Robert Latimer
discovery.note: Made at Berkeley by bombarding californium with boron nuclei.

nameOrigin: Ernest Lawrence, inventor of the cyclotron.

elementalForm.description: Never made in bulk. Its outermost electron is in a 7p orbital, a relativistic effect, rather than 6d as simple rules predict.

originNote: Made in particle accelerators.
summary: Lawrencium is the last actinide. In 2015 its first ionization energy was measured, one atom at a time, at 4.96 eV.
facts: Its ionization energy was measured in 2015 using single atoms at a time.

name: Rutherfordium

discovery.by: Albert Ghiorso and team (Berkeley); claimed by Georgy Flerov's team (Dubna) in 1964
discovery.note: IUPAC credited both labs.

nameOrigin: Ernest Rutherford, who discovered the atomic nucleus.

elementalForm.description: Made only a few atoms at a time; gas-phase experiments show it behaves like hafnium, as a group 4 metal should.

originNote: Made in particle accelerators by fusing lighter nuclei.
summary: Rutherfordium is the first transactinide element. Its chemistry, tested on single atoms, resembles hafnium's.
facts: Its naming was part of the 'Transfermium Wars' over who discovered elements 104–109.

name: Dubnium

discovery.by: Albert Ghiorso and team (Berkeley); Georgy Flerov's team (Dubna, 1968)
discovery.note: IUPAC credited both labs and named it after Dubna.

nameOrigin: Dubna, Russia, home of the Joint Institute for Nuclear Research.

elementalForm.description: Studied only one atom at a time; it behaves as a group 5 element, like niobium and tantalum.

originNote: Made in particle accelerators.
summary: Dubnium is a synthetic group 5 element. Some of its isotopes live for hours, long enough for chemistry on single atoms.
facts: Its name was disputed for decades; Americans proposed 'hahnium'.

name: Seaborgium

discovery.by: Albert Ghiorso; Kenneth Hulet and team (Berkeley-Livermore)
discovery.note: Made by bombarding californium-249 with oxygen-18.

nameOrigin: Glenn Seaborg, co-discoverer of ten elements.

elementalForm.description: Single-atom chemistry shows group 6 behavior like tungsten, including a volatile carbonyl Sg(CO)6.

originNote: Made in particle accelerators.
summary: Seaborgium was the first element named after a living person. Chemists have made its hexacarbonyl, one molecule at a time.
facts: Glenn Seaborg could write his address using element names: seaborgium, lawrencium, berkelium, californium, americium.

name: Bohrium

discovery.by: Peter Armbruster; Gottfried Münzenberg and team (GSI Darmstadt)
discovery.note: Made by fusing bismuth-209 with chromium-54.

nameOrigin: Niels Bohr.

elementalForm.description: Single atoms formed the oxychloride BhO3Cl, behaving like rhenium.

originNote: Made in particle accelerators.
summary: Bohrium is a synthetic group 7 element whose single-atom chemistry matches rhenium.
facts: Only a few dozen bohrium atoms have ever been made.

name: Hassium

discovery.by: Peter Armbruster; Gottfried Münzenberg and team (GSI Darmstadt)
discovery.note: Made by fusing lead-208 with iron-58.

nameOrigin: Hesse (Latin Hassia), the German state where GSI is located.

radioactive.note: Sits at a predicted 'doubly magic' deformed nucleus.

elementalForm.description: In 2001 chemists made hassium tetroxide, HsO4, from single atoms: it behaves like osmium tetroxide.

bulk.note: Predicted; possibly the densest element (about 41 g/cm³).

originNote: Made in particle accelerators.
summary: Hassium is predicted to be one of the densest elements, about 25% denser than osmium. Its tetroxide, HsO4, behaves much like osmium tetroxide.
facts: Hassium tetroxide was made and studied one molecule at a time in 2001.

name: Meitnerium

discovery.by: Peter Armbruster; Gottfried Münzenberg and team (GSI Darmstadt)
discovery.note: A single atom was detected after a week of bombarding bismuth with iron.

nameOrigin: Lise Meitner, co-discoverer of nuclear fission.

elementalForm.description: No chemistry has been done yet; it is predicted to behave like iridium.

originNote: Made in particle accelerators.
summary: Meitnerium honors Lise Meitner, who helped explain nuclear fission. Its properties are known only from calculations.
facts: It is the only element named solely after a real woman; curium honors Marie and Pierre Curie together.

name: Darmstadtium

discovery.note: Made by fusing lead-208 with nickel-62.

nameOrigin: Darmstadt, Germany.

elementalForm.description: No chemistry yet; predicted to resemble platinum.

originNote: Made in particle accelerators.
summary: Darmstadtium is a synthetic element predicted to be a dense noble metal like platinum.
facts: It was first made at GSI in Darmstadt, which also found elements 107–112.

name: Roentgenium

discovery.note: Made by fusing bismuth-209 with nickel-64.

nameOrigin: Wilhelm Conrad Röntgen, discoverer of X-rays.

elementalForm.description: No chemistry yet; predicted to be a noble metal below gold, perhaps even more resistant to reaction.

originNote: Made in particle accelerators.
appearance: Never seen; predicted to be silvery rather than golden.
summary: Roentgenium sits below gold. Relativistic effects are predicted to make it silvery rather than golden.
facts: It was first made exactly 99 years after Röntgen discovered X-rays (1895 to 1994).

name: Copernicium

discovery.note: Made by fusing lead-208 with zinc-70.

nameOrigin: Nicolaus Copernicus.

elementalForm.description: Single-atom experiments show copernicium binds only weakly to gold, behaving like a very volatile metal; calculations suggest it is a liquid near room temperature.

originNote: Made in particle accelerators.
summary: Copernicium is in mercury's group. Calculations predict that, like mercury, it would be a liquid metal near room temperature.
facts: It was officially named on 19 February 2010, Copernicus's 537th birthday.

name: Nihonium

discovery.note: Only three atoms were found in nine years of experiments.

nameOrigin: Nihon, Japan.

elementalForm.description: Little chemistry known; predicted to be a soft metal below thallium.

originNote: Made in particle accelerators.
summary: Nihonium was the first element discovered in Asia.
facts: The RIKEN team needed about nine years of experiments to observe three atoms.

name: Flerovium

discovery.note: Made by fusing plutonium-244 with calcium-48.

nameOrigin: The Flerov Laboratory of Nuclear Reactions, named after Georgy Flerov.

elementalForm.description: Single-atom experiments suggest flerovium is a volatile metal that bonds only weakly, partly because its 7p electrons are stabilized by relativistic effects.

originNote: Made in particle accelerators.
summary: Flerovium sits near the predicted 'island of stability' where superheavy nuclei might live longer.
facts: Its longest-lived confirmed isotope, flerovium-289, has a half-life of about 2 seconds, far longer than many lighter superheavy isotopes, a hint of the island of stability.

name: Moscovium

discovery.by: Yuri Oganessian and team (Dubna) with Lawrence Livermore
discovery.note: Made by fusing americium-243 with calcium-48.

nameOrigin: The Moscow region, where Dubna is located.

elementalForm.description: Predicted to be a heavy post-transition metal like bismuth, possibly favoring the +1 state.

originNote: Made in particle accelerators.
summary: Moscovium is a synthetic element whose chemistry has only just begun to be probed, one atom at a time.
facts: It was officially named in 2016 along with nihonium, tennessine and oganesson.

name: Livermorium

discovery.by: Yuri Oganessian and team (Dubna) with Lawrence Livermore
discovery.note: Made by fusing curium-248 with calcium-48.

nameOrigin: Lawrence Livermore National Laboratory, California.

elementalForm.description: Predicted to be a metal below polonium.

originNote: Made in particle accelerators.
summary: Livermorium is a synthetic element. In 2024 Berkeley made it with a titanium-50 beam, a step toward making element 120.
facts: Making it with a titanium-50 beam in 2024 showed a possible route to elements 119 and 120.

name: Tennessine

discovery.by: Yuri Oganessian and team (Dubna) with Oak Ridge and Vanderbilt
discovery.note: Made by fusing berkelium-249 (from Oak Ridge) with calcium-48.

nameOrigin: Tennessee, home of Oak Ridge National Laboratory and Vanderbilt University.

elementalForm.description: Though in the halogen group, it is predicted to behave more like a metalloid than like iodine.

originNote: Made in particle accelerators.
summary: Tennessine is the second-heaviest known element. Its target, berkelium-249, had to be made in a reactor and flown to Russia within months.
facts: The '-ine' ending marks it as part of the halogen group.

name: Oganesson

discovery.by: Yuri Oganessian and team (Dubna) with Lawrence Livermore
discovery.note: Made by fusing californium-249 with calcium-48; reported in 2006.

nameOrigin: Yuri Oganessian, pioneer of superheavy-element research.

radioactive.note: The only isotope seen; only five or so atoms detected.

elementalForm.description: Although in the noble-gas group, relativistic effects are predicted to make oganesson reactive and a solid semiconductor at room temperature.

originNote: Made in particle accelerators.
summary: Oganesson is the heaviest element known. Only a handful of its atoms have ever been made, each lasting under a millisecond.
facts: It is one of only two elements named after a living person (with seaborgium).
